explanations.explanation: Mercy is the very first thing out of his mouth: "Be merciful to me, O God…" (Psalm 56:1). David doesn't open with a speech or a plan. He just asks, plain and honest, like a man who knows exactly who to call. Good instincts, friend.

Wisdom is a fine thing to ask for, but it's not what David asks for first. His first words are "Be merciful to me, O God…" (Psalm 56:1). The heading says the Philistines seized him in Gath, and mercy is what he opens with. I think when the walls are closing in, asking for the big thing first makes sense.

Strength sounds like a good guess for a man in trouble, but David doesn't ask for it first. He says, "Be merciful to me, O God…" (Psalm 56:1). He goes to God for mercy before anything else. Not a muscle request in the whole opening line.
Not quite, friend. David says, "My enemies pursue me all day long, for many proudly assail me." (Psalm 56:2). Many, not a few. That's a whole crowd, and they pursue him all day long.
False is right. David says, "…for many proudly assail me." (Psalm 56:2). Many of them, and they pursue him all day long. That's not a couple of guys, that's a whole parking lot of trouble.
That's it, baker. David says, "When I am afraid, I put my trust in You." (Psalm 56:3). Notice he doesn't pretend the fear isn't there. The fear shows up, and the trust shows up right behind it.
Hiding is what I'd do, believe me. But David doesn't say that. He says, "When I am afraid, I put my trust in You." (Psalm 56:3). His answer to fear is trust, and he says it right to God.

David does go to the wilderness in other places, like 1 Samuel 23:14, but not in this verse. Here he says, "When I am afraid, I put my trust in You." (Psalm 56:3). When the fear comes, he turns toward God. Keep your running shoes in the closet for this one.

Right. David trusts God, says he will not be afraid, and then asks, "What can man do to me?" (Psalm 56:4). He's weighing the people against the God he trusts, and the people come up short. It's a question that already knows its answer.

Oh no, friend. These folks mean plenty of harm. David says they hound him, and later he says they wait "…to take my life." (Psalm 56:6). His question, "What can man do to me?" (Psalm 56:4), isn't about them being gentle. It's about trusting God over them.

I wish, but nothing in this psalm says they'll listen to anybody. David says all day long they twist his words (Psalm 56:5). So when he asks, "What can man do to me?" (Psalm 56:4), he's leaning on God, not on talking them down.
Yep, twist. David says, "All day long they twist my words…" (Psalm 56:5). He says something, and they bend it into something else. I think that gets old fast.

Praise is something David does with God's word: "In God, whose word I praise…" (Psalm 56:4). The word for his enemies here is different. He says, "All day long they twist my words…" (Psalm 56:5). Twist is the one that fits the blank.
Trust is what David does with God: "…in God I trust." (Psalm 56:4). The blank is about his enemies, and David says, "All day long they twist my words…" (Psalm 56:5). Twist is the word that fits.

True, and it's a heavy one. David says they "…watch my steps while they wait to take my life." (Psalm 56:6). This part of the psalm is serious, and David treats it that way. That's also why his trust in God matters so much here.

I wish it were false, friend, but it's true. David says they "…watch my steps while they wait to take my life." (Psalm 56:6). It's a heavy line. David is facing something real, and he takes it to God.
Cast down is right. David prays, "In Your anger, O God, cast down the nations." (Psalm 56:7). Notice who he's asking: he says it to God. Cast down is the request.
Lift up is the opposite direction, baker. David prays, "In Your anger, O God, cast down the nations." (Psalm 56:7). He's asking God to cast them down. Down, not up.

Gathering in sounds friendly, but that's not the prayer. David says, "In Your anger, O God, cast down the nations." (Psalm 56:7). It comes right after he asks if they'll escape their sin. Cast down is the request.
Not at all, friend. David says, "You have taken account of my wanderings." (Psalm 56:8). God is keeping track, not losing track. David's not lost in God's eyes for one minute.
False is right. David says, "You have taken account of my wanderings." (Psalm 56:8). God has them counted. That's a comfort, especially for anybody who has felt like nobody's keeping track.
Tears it is. David says, "Put my tears in Your bottle…" (Psalm 56:8). He's asking God to hold on to them. I think that's one of the tenderest lines in the whole psalm.
David does write songs, and this is one. But the verse says something different: "Put my tears in Your bottle…" (Psalm 56:8). Tears are what he asks God to keep.
Prayers is a good guess, since this whole psalm is a prayer. But David says, "Put my tears in Your bottle…" (Psalm 56:8). It's his tears he wants God to hold.
Retreat, baker. David says, "Then my enemies will retreat on the day I cry for help." (Psalm 56:9). The day he calls out is the day they back off. That's some powerful backup.

Surrounding him is what you'd expect from this crowd, but that's not what David says. He says, "Then my enemies will retreat on the day I cry for help." (Psalm 56:9). When he cries out, they pull back.
Laughing isn't in this verse, friend. David says, "Then my enemies will retreat on the day I cry for help." (Psalm 56:9). The word is retreat. On the day he cries for help, they pull back.
True. David says, "By this I will know that God is on my side." (Psalm 56:9). The retreat of his enemies is how he'll know. He's looking for that sign.
Not false, friend. David says, "By this I will know that God is on my side." (Psalm 56:9). He's sure of it. He says he'll know it when his enemies retreat.

Thank offerings, yes. David says, "Your vows are upon me, O God; I will render thank offerings to You." (Psalm 56:12). He mentions the vows and the thank offerings side by side. That's a grateful man right there.
Gold and silver would look nice on the counter, but David doesn't mention either. He says, "I will render thank offerings to You." (Psalm 56:12). Thanks is what he plans to bring.
A new altar is a big project, baker, and David doesn't say anything about building one. He says, "I will render thank offerings to You." (Psalm 56:12). Thank offerings are what he brings.
Death, and David says it plainly: "For You have delivered my soul from death…" (Psalm 56:13). Remember the enemies waiting to take his life (Psalm 56:6). Now he's giving thanks for being delivered.
Shame is a heavy thing, but that's not the word David uses. He says, "For You have delivered my soul from death…" (Psalm 56:13). That's the deliverance he thanks God for.
Hunger is a real struggle, but David doesn't say it here. He says, "For You have delivered my soul from death…" (Psalm 56:13). Death is the thing God delivered him from.

explanations.answer: Walk before God in the light of life
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. David says God delivered him "…that I may walk before God in the light of life." (Psalm 56:13). He's out of the dark and walking in the light. After a psalm full of fear, that's a good place to land.

explanations.answer: Rest in God's house for the length of days
explanations.explanation: That's a lovely line, and it's a different psalm. David says in Psalm 23:6, "…I will dwell in the house of the LORD for the length of my days." Here he says God delivered him "…that I may walk before God in the light of life." (Psalm 56:13). Walking, not resting.

explanations.answer: Stand among his people in the city gate
explanations.explanation: The city gate is a fine spot, but it's not in this psalm. David says God delivered him "…that I may walk before God in the light of life." (Psalm 56:13). Walking in the light is the goal here.
